Clinical actions cannot exceed available staff capacity.

assumptions: The initial hospital capacity is exactly 40 licensed beds and the initial ventilator inventory is exactly 6, as stated.
The simulation begins with 36 occupied beds and 4 available beds; this is an estimate representing a hospital already experiencing a surge.
The initial 36 hospitalized patients are modeled as flu patients; this is a simplification.
The initial arrival rate is estimated at 5 flu patients per day.
The initial probability that a newly arriving flu patient needs ventilation is estimated at 15%.
The initial daily probability that a hospitalized patient newly develops ventilation need is estimated at 5%.
The initial average hospital stay is estimated at 7 days.
The initial daily recovery probability is estimated at 10%, and the initial daily death risks are estimated at 25% without needed ventilation and 8% with needed ventilation.
The hospital is assumed to have 20 clinical staff members, with capacity for 120 patient-care tasks per day and a 1% daily absence probability per staff member.
Each ventilated patient uses exactly one ventilator continuously during a tick.
Ventilator failure is estimated at 0.1% per ventilator per day, and repair takes 3 days.
The supplier initially has 20 ventilators, can accept at most 10 units per day for this hospital, and has a 7-day delivery lead time.
New ventilators are assumed to be functional upon delivery.
Deaths, recoveries, and discharges immediately free the associated bed and ventilator at the end of the tick.
The allocation policy is an explicit decision variable; the model does not assume first-come-first-served unless selected by the administrator.

Patient arrivals, disease progression, recovery, death, staff absence, and equipment failure are stochastic events whose probabilities apply independently within each daily tick unless a policy specifies otherwise.
No ventilator sharing, partial ventilation, external hospital transfer, or emergency bed expansion is modeled unless added as a scenario option.
Orders are placed at the end of a tick and become usable after the full stated lead time.

state.unit: probability per day per staff member

processes_each_tick: New flu patients arrive at the hospital according to the incoming patient arrival rate, subject to available beds and daily admission capacity.
Each hospitalized patient advances one day in illness and remaining length of stay decreases by one day.
Patients whose illness progresses develop a need for ventilation according to their individual ventilation-need probability.
Patients who need ventilation but do not receive it face their untreated daily death risk; patients receiving needed ventilation face their treated daily death risk.
Patients may recover according to their recovery probability, leave the hospital when their length of stay reaches zero, and free a bed and ventilator if they were using one.
Deaths remove patients, free occupied beds, and free any ventilators they were using.
Ventilated patients consume one ventilator continuously for the tick.
Each functional ventilator in use or standby may fail according to its failure rate; failed ventilators leave service for their repair time.
Absent staff are removed from available staffing capacity, and available staff capacity limits admissions and patient-care tasks.
Ordered ventilators whose lead time has elapsed are delivered, added to owned and functional ventilator counts, and increase hospital ventilator capacity.
Patients denied admission because no bed or care capacity is available remain outside the hospital as unmet demand and face an estimated daily deterioration risk.
odd.purpose: The simulation answers how ventilator-allocation policies and ventilator orders affect survival, bed occupancy, and unmet ventilation demand during a flu surge.

scenario_text: A 40-bed hospital with 6 ventilators faces a flu surge; staff decide who gets ventilated and whether to order more.

targeted_repair.problem: Extreme-conditions test (Sterman): with hospital-ventilators functional_count at zero, the model shows no consequence for patients who need ventilation: no deterioration and no deaths, although the patient group has daily_death_risk_without_needed_ventilation. Also a ventilator can be assigned when no functional ventilator is free. Fix: (1) add a process by which patients who need ventilation but are not ventilated die (patient_count and occupied_beds fall, available_beds rise) each tick; (2) assigning a ventilator must require that functional_count exceeds in_use_count.

rule.rationale: Each tick, one patient dies when the cohort needs ventilation, remains unventilated, and has a positive represented mortality risk.

checks.label: the patients face a risk of death without ventilation

rule.rationale: Clinical staff can assign a colocated ventilator only when the selected stock has a functional unit not already in use.

checks.label: the ventilators are with the clinical staff
the patients are with the clinical staff

limits: Ventilation status is cohort-level, so it cannot distinguish partially ventilated patients within one group.
Only single-ventilator assignments are offered to match the free-unit check.
The legacy assign-ventilators action cannot inspect ventilator stock because it has no ventilator participant.
tests: Clinical staff can assign one colocated ventilator when functional count exceeds in-use count.
Assignment increases the selected ventilator stock's in-use count and marks the patients ventilated.
Assignment is refused when functional count equals in-use count.
Assignment is refused when functional count is zero.
Patients not marked as needing ventilation are refused.
Ventilators or patients at another location are refused.
semantic_bindings: the acting clinical staff perform the assignment
ventilators is the equipment stock used by the staff

proposal.why: This adds a recurring death consequence for patients awaiting ventilation and prevents stock-aware assignment without a free functional ventilator; hospital bed totals cannot lawfully be updated by that patient process because processes may affect only their selected entity and the hospital is a separate entity.
